/-!
# Erdős Problem 275

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/275](https://www.erdosproblems.com/275)
- [CrVE70] R.B. Crittenden and C.L. Vanden Eynden, *Any n arithmetic progressions covering the first
  2^n integers cover all integers*, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 24 (1970), 475-481.
-/

open Set

namespace Erdos275

/--
If a finite system of $r$ congruences $\{ a_i\pmod{n_i} : 1\leq i\leq r\}$ (the $n_i$ are not
necessarily distinct) covers $2^r$ consecutive integers then it covers all integers.

This is best possible as the system $2^{i-1}\pmod{2^i}$ shows. This was proved independently by
Selfridge and Crittenden and Vanden Eynden [CrVE70].

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos275.lean"]
theorem erdos_275 (r : ℕ) (a : Fin r → ℤ) (n : Fin r → ℕ)
    (H : ∃ k : ℤ, ∀ x ∈ Ico k (k + 2 ^ r), ∃ i, x ≡ a i [ZMOD n i]) (x : ℤ) :
    ∃ i, x ≡ a i [ZMOD n i] := by
  sorry

end Erdos275

reformulations.difference: The Lean theorem permits zero moduli through `n : Fin r → ℕ`, whereas the original paper explicitly assumes positive moduli.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Modulo zero, Int.ModEq means equality. To derive the unrestricted theorem from its positive-modulus version, fix the target integer x and replace each zero modulus at index i by |a_i − x| + 1. Every originally covered integer remains covered: the original zero-modulus class was just {a_i}. Apply the positive-modulus theorem to this replacement system. If x is covered by a replacement class, divisibility by a modulus greater than |a_i − x| forces x = a_i, so the original zero-modulus class also covers x. The reverse implication follows by restriction. This universal equivalence was proved independently in scratch.lean without using the reviewed theorem's sorry.

reformulations.difference: The original paper states a contrapositive for the first 2^r positive integers; Lean states that covering any block of 2^r consecutive integers implies covering all integers, as does the Erdős webpage.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Take the contrapositive and translate a block beginning at k by subtracting k − 1 from both integers and residues. The interval Ico k (k + 2^r) becomes precisely {1,…,2^r}, and congruence is preserved. Conversely, specialize the covering statement to k = 1 and take its contrapositive. The equivalence, combined with the zero-modulus reduction, was proved in scratch.lean.
